catalog_quote: [p. 69] The high central vowel /ɨ/ is neutral in regard to tongue root position. It is lax but is not considered to be [-ATR], since it does not participate in the vowel harmony system (cf. section 5.1). /ɨ/ occurs in morphemes which are never stressed such as prefixes and proclitic grammatical particles: [p. 70] /mɨ-/ + /tɔ́nɔ́/ --> /mɨtɔ́nɔ́/ 'nominalizer' 'begin' 'beginning' ... It usually occurs in the unstressed antepenultimate syllable of stems consisting of more than two syllables: [bɨ̀lúndù] /bɨ̀lúndù/ 'grandfather' ... However, there are a few examples in which a vowel other than /ɨ/ occurs in the antepenultimate syllable, e.g. /mbɔ́lífɔ́/ 'pigeon' and /gbɛ̀gbɛ́rì/ 'throat'. ... [sec. 3. TONE, p. 70] Baka has a two-register tone system. The following are examples of minimal contrasts and of all four possible sequences (high-high, high-low, low-high, low-low): ... [note 5, p. 84] Considering the slim evidence for treating [ɨ] as a phoneme, it is not impossible that a stress rule or a morphophonemic rule could be found to handle [ɨ] as a reduced allophone of some underlying vowel. Even when a proclitic occurs in isolation the [ɨ] may be considered to be a morphologically conditioned reduced form.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Baka is described as a two-tone (H/L) language; Parker gives no rule for where stress falls. The only stress information is negative/impressionistic: prefixes and proclitics are never stressed, and in trisyllabic stems (presyllable + CVCV root) the antepenultimate presyllable is unstressed, implying prominence lies within the final disyllabic root, locus unspecified.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; Parker notes a few words with a full (non-ɨ) vowel in the antepenultimate syllable (/mbɔ́lífɔ́/ 'pigeon', /gbɛ̀gbɛ́rì/ 'throat') but says nothing about their stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remarks made in passing within the vowel description; sentence-level intonation (sec. 6) separately notes extra-high pitch on penultimate syllables in questions. No dedicated stress/accent section exists in the article.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to Baka of South Sudan (Maridi area; ISO bdh, Glottolog baka1274, Central Sudanic, Bongo-Baka group) -- not the Ubangian Baka of Cameroon/Gabon (bkc). Parker's data are from Maridi (acknowledging Edward Mandeson, IRL Maridi); no dialect differentiation is made. The Tucker & Bryan 1966 stress remark is a Bongo-Bagirmi group-level statement illustrated with Bagirmi, not a Baka statement.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Bongo-Bagirmi group as a whole (Baka is a member): stress normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, always so when the second syllable has a 'semi-mute' (reduced) vowel; occasionally on the second syllable when the first has a central vowel. No Baka-specific statement and no rule for words of three or more syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Second-syllable stress when the first syllable contains a central vowel (Stevenson's Bagirmi kala 'snake').
new_statements.identity_note: All items concern Baka of South Sudan (Maridi area), ISO bdh, Central Sudanic, Bongo-Bagirmi (Bongo-Baka) group, not the Ubangian Baka of Cameroon/Gabon. The Tucker & Bryan 1966 stress paragraph is a generalization over the whole Bongo-Bagirmi group (Bagirmi, Sara, Kresh, Bongo, Baka, etc.), with its example from Stevenson's Bagirmi manuscript; the chapter's Baka data come from Tucker's own notes and Santandrea. new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages (chapter sources: Tucker's field notes, Stevenson's Bagirmi/Sara MSS, Santandrea's Bongo-group sketches): in disyllabic words stress normally falls on the first syllable, and always does when the second syllable has a semi-mute (barely articulated final) vowel; occasionally the second syllable is stressed when the first contains a central vowel (Bagirmi kala 'snake'). The chapter treats the languages as tonal (2a: three levels noted in Bongo, Baka, Morokodo, Kresh, Yulu, Kara, Sara Mbai, partly Bagirmi). Baka is not named in the stress paragraph, but sec. 1 says semi-mute vowels among the Eastern languages are confined to Bongo and Baka.

new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern Baka of South Sudan (Maridi area), ISO bdh, Central Sudanic > Bongo-Bagirmi (Tucker's 'Bongo-Baka(-Bagirmi) group'); not Baka of Cameroon/Gabon (bkc) - the endangeredvoices.org and academia 'Baka wordlist' search hits are the Cameroon language and were discarded. Tucker & Bryan's stress sentence is a generalisation over the Bongo-Bagirmi group, not a Baka-specific observation.

readall_conflicts: No source states a Baka-specific stress-placement rule. Parker 1985 (already in the catalog) describes a two-register H/L tone system and mentions stress only in passing: prefixes and proclitic particles are 'never stressed', and /ɨ/ 'usually occurs in the unstressed antepenultimate syllable of stems consisting of more than two syllables'. Tucker & Bryan 1966 (snippets only, no page number) give a group-level rule for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages: initial stress in disyllables, second-syllable stress occasionally when the first syllable has a central vowel, illustrated with Bagirmi. These two are not in direct contradiction (different word lengths, different scope: language-specific aside vs. group generalization) but do not add up to a single stated rule; both would be consistent with penultimate stress, which no source claims. Tucker 1940 and Sampson 1997 contributed nothing (snippets without a stress remark; not accessible). No contradiction among the sources opened. The catalog codes Baka 'tonal' with no placement rule (Parker 1985: two-register tone system; stress mentioned only in passing - /ɨ/ in never-stressed prefixes and in the 'unstressed antepenultimate syllable' of trisyllabic stems). Tucker & Bryan 1966 add a GROUP-level default for Bongo-Bagirmi (stress normally on the first syllable of disyllables, exceptions when the first vowel is central), recovered only from search snippets and illustrated with Bagirmi, not Baka; it is compatible with the tonal coding and…
